_: Works Charlie keeps by eye, against the automatic gates. A rescue is written down here rather than paid for by widening a threshold — a threshold moved to admit one picture admits everything else in the same band, and nobody counts what that let in. Prose: research/2026-08-19-funnel-and-overrules.md
reads: The funnel sheet lifts these out of whatever pile they landed in and shows them under 'rescued by hand', with the gate that had dropped them still named.
companion: references.json — that file is what thresholds are calibrated to KEEP; this file is what they failed to keep and Charlie kept anyway.
batch_2026-08-19: Eleven works picked off the funnel sheet, no reason given for any of them beyond wanting them. The `fails` line on each is measured, not guessed — it is the gate that actually dropped that work on the run he was looking at. Three patterns run through them and are worth reading together: four die on the name filter because a myth or a Welsh lake reads as a person, four die on the warm ceiling by between 0.008 and 0.15, three die at the dark end of the box (off too low, cap too high, busy far over).
batch_2026-08-19_gallery: Ten works ALREADY IN THE GALLERY, added at Charlie's request 'so they don't disappear'. A different kind of entry from the ones above: those are works a gate rejected and he wants anyway, these already shipped and he wants them protected from any later re-selection. Six he named outright; four are the ruins/pantheon set he confirmed when asked which 'the 4 favorites' meant. Four of the ten fail something today and six pass everything; all ten are listed, because an entry saying 'nothing drops this' is what stops someone re-checking it next month.
batch_2026-08-19_sheet: Six works picked off the /dark preview sheet, marked `from: the /dark sheet`. Charlie asked for 'these five' and then named six titles; all six are here, because dropping one to make the count match would mean guessing which. NONE of them is rejected by anything today — they are all survivors of the whole chain — so every one of these entries is protection against a future tightening rather than a rescue from a present gate. Three carry no model verdict. Two of them, the John Martin and the van Schrieck, sit within 0.07 of the warm ceiling, which is inside the band the profile problem described below can move a work across; a third, the Blumenstück, is already over it on its source file and under it on the plate.
which_surface: MEASUREMENT SURFACE MATTERS HERE AND IT DID NOT USED TO. Every number in this file was previously read off the harvest's 400 px plate, and that is the surface the box actually judges on. While measuring this batch it turned out that the intake DROPPED THE ICC PROFILE instead of converting to sRGB, so for the ~60% of Cleveland files that carry one, the plate reads about 17% cooler and 8% less colourful than the museum's own file. So each entry below carries `measured` — the plate, the surface the gates use — and, where they differ, `museum` — the file the plate came from. Neither is decoration: Ruin by the Sea passes the warm ceiling on one and fails it on the other. Full measurement: research/2026-08-19-the-plate-is-not-the-painting.md. NOT on the plate in images/plates/, which is already desaturated and dimmed and would give the box's reading of the treatment rather than of the painting.

keep.title: Two Hummingbirds and an Orchid
keep.why: Charlie: 'that two hummingbird orchid is really cool'. The pale ground is exactly what the brightness measures are built to catch — median luma 180 against a reference envelope topping out at 78, caption contrast 1.77 — so no luma ceiling that does its job will ever admit it. It is the same work he had questioned that morning ('those hummingbirds passed the brightness filters?'), and the later verdict is the one that stands.
keep.fails: Nothing in the snapshot box, whose luma ceiling is 200 — which is how it reached the sheet at all. It fails any luma ceiling worth setting (78 or 85) and every caption floor. It also dies on the name filter when that gate is fed the raw Wikimedia file name, which begins 'Martin Johnson Heade'.
keep.identification: Three works on the sheet answer to 'two hummingbirds' and an orchid. This is the one the conversation was about: the luma-180 plate. The other two sit at luma 80 and 85 and are not at issue.

keep.title: In the Woods
keep.why: Charlie's pick, already shipped. Also one of the eight in references.json, which makes it the only work that is both a calibration reference and a hand overrule — the set the thresholds are fitted to contains a work the thresholds reject.
keep.fails: box on two counts: warm 0.718 against a ceiling of 0.47 — by a long way, this is the warmest work in either reference file — and cap 12.8 against a ceiling of 11. It is the one of the eight the snapshot box already loses, which is recorded in research/2026-08-19-reference-sets.md.
keep.harvest: not in this harvest, so no plate exists — the numbers above are the museum's own print file, which is a slightly different surface from the one the gates judge on
keep.discrepancy: references.json has cap 10.68 for this work and 0.717 for warm. Warm agrees to a thousandth; cap does not — 12.8 here against 10.68 there. cap is read off the single brightest of 24 caption cells, so it moves with which museum rendition was fetched, and the eight in references.json turn out not to have all been measured on the same one (see research/2026-08-19-the-plate-is-not-the-painting.md). Both numbers fail the ceiling of 11 either way, so nothing here turns on it, and references.json has NOT been edited: overwriting a calibration value from a differently-sourced measurement is how a reference set stops being one.

keep.title: Ruin by the Sea

keep.fails: nothing on the plate — warm 0.466 clears the ceiling of 0.47 by 0.004 — and warm on the museum file, where 0.624 misses it by 0.154. It is the ONE work in a 39-work sample that changes sides on the box's only binding bound depending on which surface is measured.
keep.harvest: in this harvest as cle-1979.57, and it survives the chain — on the plate
keep.why_it_matters: research/2026-08-19-reference-sets.md justifies the ceiling of 0.47 by saying it 'sits just above Ruin by the Sea at 0.465'. That reading is the profile-stripped one. On the museum's own file the work is at 0.624, so the ceiling does not sit just above it — it sits well below it, and the stated reason for putting the ceiling at 0.47 does not survive. Nothing has been changed on the strength of this; it is written down so the next person to touch the warm bound knows what it was anchored to.
